extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; critics and essayists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging or emulating the qualities of English essays and periodical papers (style, humour, moral tone, invention, narrative unity) as exemplified by Joseph Addison and the Spectator series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and arrangement of words (diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mere choice and arrangement of his words would have sufficed to make his essays classical... the English language been written with such sweetness, grace, and facility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer diction that combines sweetness, grace, and facility; wording and sentence arrangement should themselves elevate the essay toward classical quality. Examples: clear, elegant phrasing that reads effortlessly; avoid over-laboured or clumsy constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation of life and character
rubrics_metrics.description: “As an observer of life, of manners, of all the shades of human character, he stands in the first class.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce acute, varied, and truthful portraits of manners and character. Aim for vividness rivaling great dramatists/novelists (Shakspeare, Cervantes). Use concrete detail and specific incidents to reveal personality rather than abstract description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of invention and fable (imaginative material)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The numerous fictions, generally original, often wild and grotesque, but always singularly graceful and happy, which are found in his essays, fully entitle him to the rank of a great poet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include original fictions, allegories, or apologues that are inventive and gracefully told. Varied imaginative forms (allegory, apologue, portrait) strengthen an essayist’s range. Strive for felicitous invention rather than forced novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour: tone and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison’s humour: “a look of demure serenity, disturbed only by an arch sparkle of the eye... His tone is never that either of a Jack Pudding or of a Cynic. It is that of a gentleman… tempered by good nature and good breeding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for humour that is restrained, urbane, and humane rather than coarse, buffoonish, or misanthropic. The comic effect should be produced without grossness or personal malignity—an arch, cultivated tone is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral temper of satire (ethical restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: “That which chiefly distinguishes Addison... is the grace, the nobleness, the moral purity, which we find even in his merriment... it would be difficult... to find... a single taunt which can be called ungenerous or unkind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should correct vice without degrading persons; maintain compassion and reverence even while ridiculing follies. Avoid personal lampoons and vindictive attacks; satire’s highest effect is to reform, not to ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original voice / inimitability
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of the many eminent men who have made Addison their model... none has been able to catch the tone of his pleasantry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a distinctive, authentic voice rather than mere imitation of diction. A memorable tone combines manner, moral stance, and temperament in a way that is hard to copy; originality in voice is a high mark of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and freshness across a series
rubrics_metrics.description: “His invention never seems to flag; nor is he ever under the necessity of repeating himself, or of wearing out a subject. There are no dregs in his wine. ... On the Monday we have an allegory... on the Tuesday an Eastern apologue... on the Saturday a religious meditation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across many essays or instalments, sustain inventiveness and avoid repetition. Rotate forms and subjects (allegory, apologue, character sketch, scene, meditation) so readers receive a fresh pleasure in each piece; economy—withdraw a joke before it grows stale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural unity and narrative coherence in serial essays
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every valuable essay in the series may be read with pleasure separately; yet the five or six hundred essays form a whole, and a whole which has the interest of a novel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing many short pieces, aim for both standalone worth and cumulative unity: recurring characters, linked episodes, and a loose narrative arc can give the series novel-like interest without forcing artificial plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-creation and portraiture (dramatic immediacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He could call human beings into existence, and make them exhibit themselves... If we wish to find anything more vivid than Addison’s best portraits, we must go either to Shakspeare or to Cervantes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who act and speak so vividly that they seem to exist independently. Use concrete actions, dialogues, and idiosyncratic detail to let personality emerge; prefer showing to telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of seriousness and pleasantry (moral seriousness paired with wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: “His mirth consistent with tender compassion for all that is frail, and with profound reverence for all that is sublime... Nothing great, nothing amiable... has ever been associated by Addison with any degrading idea.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair lightness with moral seriousness: a writer can be witty while preserving reverence for the sublime and humane regard for people. Avoid trivializing important themes for cheap laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of tone to audience and intimacy (conversational realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: “To enjoy his conversation in the highest perfection, it was necessary to be alone with him... ‘There is no such thing,’ he used to say, ‘as real conversation, but between two persons.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone to audience: choose an intimate, conversational register for close, reflective pieces and a more public tone for broader-address essays. Conversational realism—as of two persons talking—can yield naturalness and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre versatility (use of multiple small forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the Spectator: allegory, Eastern apologue, character, scene from common life, sly Horatian pleasantry, religious meditation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a range of short forms and modes within an essayistic project to showcase skill and keep readers engaged. Each mode has its conventions—use them knowingly (e.g., allegory for moral point, character sketch for social portrait).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and tasteful restraint (avoid excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: “As soon as we have tasted the first sparkling foam of a jest, it is withdrawn, and a fresh draught of nectar is at our lips.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice restraint: do not overplay jokes or sentiments; finish effects while they are at their best. Brevity and tasteful withholding often increase charm and perceived elegance.
